steps.message:
Ruby's parser confirms the trap. `///evil.example/phish` parses as a path (`/evil.example/phish`, host nil), but browsers read it as `http://evil.example/phish`. class SessionsController < ApplicationController
  allow_unauthenticated_access only: %i[ new create ]
  rate_limit to: 10, within: 3.minutes, only: :create, with: -> { render_rejection :too_many_requests }

  before_action :ensure_user_exists, only: :new

  def new
  end

  def create
    if user = User.active.authenticate_by(email_address: params[:email_address], password: params[:password])
      start_new_session_for user
      redirect_to safe_return_to_path || post_authenticating_url
    else
      render_rejection :unauthorized
    end
  end

  def destroy
    terminate_current_session
    redirect_to root_url
  end

  private
    def ensure_user_exists
      redirect_to first_run_url if User.none?
    end

    def render_rejection(status)
      flash[:alert] = "Too many requests or unauthorized."
      render :new, status: status
    end

    # Only send the reader to a page on this app. We keep the path and query of a relative path or of an
    # absolute URL on our own host, and redirect to that path on our host. Anything else is ignored.
    def safe_return_to_path
      return_to = params[:return_to]
      return unless return_to.is_a?(String) && return_to.present?

      # "//host" and "/\host" look like paths, but browsers treat them as a host.
      return if return_to.start_with?("//", "/\\")

      uri = URI.parse(return_to)
      if uri.scheme || uri.host
        return unless %w[ http https ].include?(uri.scheme&.downcase) && uri.host&.casecmp?(request.host) && uri.port == request.port
      end
      return unless uri.path.to_s.start_with?("/")

      uri.query ? "#{uri.path}?#{uri.query}" : uri.path
    rescue URI::InvalidURIError
      nil
    end
end
EOF

class SessionsController < ApplicationController
  allow_unauthenticated_access only: %i[ new create ]
  rate_limit to: 10, within: 3.minutes, only: :create, with: -> { render_rejection :too_many_requests }

      start_new_session_for user
      redirect_to safe_return_to_path || post_authenticating_url
    else
      render_rejection :unauthorized
    end
  end

  def destroy
    terminate_current_session
    redirect_to root_url
  end

  private
    def ensure_user_exists
      redirect_to first_run_url if User.none?
    end

    def render_rejection(status)
      flash[:alert] = "Too many requests or unauthorized."
      render :new, status: status
    end

    # Only send the reader to a page on this app. An absolute URL is accepted only if it points at our own host and
    # port. Either way we return just the path and query, which we redirect to on our host. Anything else is ignored.
    def safe_return_to_path
      return_to = params[:return_to]
      return unless return_to.is_a?(String) && return_to.present?

      uri = URI.parse(return_to)
      if uri.scheme || uri.host
        return unless %w[ http https ].include?(uri.scheme&.downcase) && uri.host&.casecmp?(request.host) && uri.port == request.port
      end

      path = [ uri.path, uri.query ].compact.join("?")
      # Browsers read "//host" and "/\host" as a host rather than a path, so only accept a path whose second character isn't a slash or backslash.
      path if path.match?(%r{\A/(?![/\\])})
    rescue URI::Error
      nil
    end
end

steps.message:
The open redirect is closed. Sign-in now only sends the reader to a page on this app, and anything else falls back to the default destination. The change is one file, `app/controllers/sessions_controller.rb`. There are no migrations and nothing under `db/`, and I didn't edit any tests.

**What was wrong:** `create` passed `params[:return_to]` straight into `redirect_to ..., allow_other_host: true`. I reproduced it: `https://evil.example/...`, `//evil.example/...` and `///evil.example/...` all sent the reader off-site after sign-in. Arrays and hashes in the parameter caused a 500.

**What it does now:**
- A relative path such as `/1/handbook?x=1` is kept.
- An absolute URL is kept only if its host and port match this app. That covers the links the app generates itself, which are absolute `request.url` values.
- Anything else is ignored, including other hosts, `//host`, `/\host`, `javascript:`, userinfo tricks, malformed input, arrays and hashes. These sign the reader in and send them to the default destination.
- Only the path and query are kept, and the redirect is built on our own host. `allow_other_host` is gone, so Rails' own open-redirect guard also applies.

**Verification:**
- `bin/rails test`: 179 runs, 0 failures, 2 skips. That matches the baseline.
- Attack payloads all land on `/`. Legitimate deep links are preserved.
- A signed-out visit to `/users?page=2` goes to sign-in, and after signing in the reader returns to `/users?page=2`.
- Wrong passwords still get a 401, and no return_to still goes to root.
- Brakeman reports one "Possible unprotected redirect" on the original code and none on the fix.
- Rubocop is clean on the changed file.

**Things to know:**
- I found one more bypass during review: `http://our-host//evil.example` passes a naive check, and Rails then crashed the sign-in with a 500. The final check looks at the path that actually gets redirected to, so that case now lands on `/`.
- I didn't add regression tests to the repo, because you asked me not to edit the test suite. My probe tests live in `/tmp/verify`, outside the repo. If you'd like permanent coverage, I can add a test file.
- The `return_to_after_authenticating` session value, used by `post_authenticating_url`, is never set anywhere in the app. Its redirect now also goes through Rails' open-redirect guard. That only matters if something starts setting it to a foreign URL.
